column5: English edition 1987 (Lawrence Hill, tr. Harold Salemson) of L'Afrique noire pre-coloniale (Presence Africaine, 1960). Diop frames it as African historical sociology, not narrative history, arguing that West African documents allow a continuous account for about 2000 years and that African 'technical lags' have objective structural causes. The text I ingested is an OCR of a scanned PDF; preface pages appear twice in the scan. Quotes from the book: none needed.

Diop describes Senegambian society as gor (nobles and farmers), neno (hereditary artisan castes) and djam (slaves of the king, of the mother's house, of the father's house), and argues that the nobility could not exploit lower castes and that royal slaves were 'slaves in name only', so no revolution occurred. Evidence is Wolof and Cayor structure plus analogies to Egypt and India. Course Module 8 weighs slavery and effects with Manning, Thornton, Nunn and Rodney; Diop's reading is a benign-structure thesis that other historians of African slavery (e.g. Lovejoy, outside these books, not verified) contest because enslaved people could be sold, killed without compensation (Diop says so himself for father's-house slaves) and exported. Show as one position and use his own words about the father's slaves as an internal check.

Diop cites Ibn Battuta (Mali in 1352) that people take names from maternal uncles and nephews, not sons, inherit, and says he saw this elsewhere only in Malabar. Confirms course Module 4 lesson 2's use of Ibn Battuta and Mali's matrilineal inheritance point (also in lesson 4 on sources). Diop also cites Ibn Khaldun and the Tarikh es-Sudan for the end of clan organisation in Ghana and Mali by the 14th century: a tidy inference, but not evidence.

Diop asserts there was no feudal system in Africa because land was sacred and not owned by nobles. Course Module 5 compares Oyo, Asante and Dahomey with land-holding, tribute and office-holding; many historians describe land tenure arrangements in African states as varied, so 'no feudalism, land belongs to no one' is a generalisation to tag [CONTESTED]. Strong point: Diop is right that European 'feudalism' is a poor template for African societies (common view in Reader/Rodney too).

Diop attributes caste in Egypt, Babylon, Africa and India to 'Cushite' influence, quoting Lenormant (1890), and the Brahmin-Dravidian argument that caste did not follow colour. The Cushite-origin claim is nineteenth-century speculation; the argument that Indian caste and Egyptian occupational classes were not simply racial is acceptable but unproven here. Not for the course.

Summary of Fustel de Coulanges (1864) on Greek and Roman class struggle, contrasted with 'African collectivism'. Diop argues Aryan 'northern cradle' peoples could not conceive a state beyond the city and that Egypt supplied the idea of empire and of a universal God (Akhenaten). Out of scope for the African course; relevant only as the comparative frame (Southern vs Northern cradle) of the whole book. Fustel is dated, and the claim that universal ideas derive from Egypt is Diop's thesis [CONTESTED]. Not used in lessons beyond a one-line description of the book's method in Module 1 historiography box.

Rapid survey of the European Middle Ages (Ribard, Vignaux) with the point that the West was technically behind the East and relied on Arab transmission (compass, gunpowder, Avicenna and Averroes). Sets up the book's comparison; out of scope for the course; the claim that Spain's early lead came from Arab contributions is a generalisation. Not used in lessons.

Diop describes the Mossi 'constitution' (Moro Naba chosen by a college of four dignitaries; togo naba prime minister from commoner families; rassam naba chief of crown slaves and finance minister; slave generals who may not ride horses) and the Cayor council (Lamane, Diawerigne representatives of free men, clergy and crown slaves/tieddo), and argues the same structure governed African states from Ghana onward. Course Module 4/5 does not cover Mossi or Cayor; this adds two worked cases of office-holding by slaves and commoners. His evidence is early-20th-century ethnography (Tauxier) and Cayor to 1870, projected back 'two thousand years': tag [CONTESTED]; the label 'constitutional monarchy' is Diop's analogy.

column4: ch-006 chunk 1 (Chapter 4, Ghana and Mali succession)
column5: Diop cites al-Bakri (1067): the Ghana king's successor is his sister's son, with an explicit reason given by informants; and Ibn Khaldun on Mali's early succession (Mari Djata, Mansa Wali, Wati, Khalifa killed as a bloody tyrant, Abu Bakr son of Mari Djata's daughter, usurper Sakura). Confirms the course's use of al-Bakri (1068, informants) and Ibn Khaldun in Module 4 and gives a succession example; Diop writes Ghana's end as 1242 by Sundiata, whereas the course keeps Kirina c.1235 as a [TRADITIONAL DATE]: show both and choose the course's tagged date.

Songhai under the Askias: succession by competition among brothers, offices bartered ('make me Balama, I will make you Askia'), generals no longer from slaves, precedence list from Kati (Tarikh al-Fattash), tin-touri ember emblem, bara-koi veto. Useful concrete detail for Module 4 lesson 3 (chronicles). Diop admits Kati and Sadi embellished Askia Muhammad's reign: a source-critique point matching the course's method.

Seven Cayor garmi dynasties with matrilineal succession, exiled pretenders (djin) returning with slaves, the kingmaker Diaraf (the course's Cayor-free Module 5 has none), immigrant kings from Mali or Songhai in the 14th century and the Macina example from the Tarikh es-Sudan. Useful as a case of states formed by exiled princes imposing a royal layer on older structures; Diop labels 'oral tradition + Tarikh', but Cayor's early history is thin and mostly known from colonial-period oral tradition [THIN EVIDENCE]; Diop also reports a 1956 conversation with Fode Diouf of Salum, an unrecorded interview, as evidence.

Diop generalises a 'vitalist' ontology (Tempels, Griaule) as the basis of kingship across Africa and says kings were killed or symbolically killed when vital force declined (Zed/Sed festival, Yoruba, Songhai, Meroe). Course lesson 4 (Module 5) treats myth as evidence of belief, not events; the Frazer-Seligman divine-kingship model of regicide is not supported by direct evidence for most of these peoples. Tag [CONTESTED]; teach at most as a historiographic example. Contrast with the course's rule to ask what a myth does.

Diop treats Ghana's king Kanissa as contemporary with the Prophet (6th century) with a capital at Koranga, a massacre of a corrupt dynasty (Kati), and a Ghana ruling from the 3rd to the 10th century. The course says Ghana is first recorded in the late 8th century (al-Fazari) and known mainly from al-Bakri 1068 and archaeology at Kumbi Saleh. The earlier dates come from Tarikh al-Fattash king-lists: [TRADITIONAL DATE] at best. Show the sources' disagreement and choose the course's cautious start date.

column4: ch-006 chunk 2 (Chapter 4, Ghana king's daily routine)
column5: Cites al-Idrisi that the Ghana king rode out daily preceded by giraffes and elephants, and that complaints were heard in person (cf. Ibn Battuta on Mali audiences). al-Idrisi is a 12th century geographer who never visited; the course already warns that al-Bakri compiled from informants. Treat the giraffe and elephant detail as hearsay; I did not re-check it against al-Idrisi.

column4: ch-006 chunk 3 (Chapter 4, Sonni Ali and Askia Muhammad)
column5: Diop contrasts the Tarikh es-Sudan's hostile portrait of Sonni Ali (c.1464) with its warm portrait of Askia Muhammad (1493), arguing Sonni Ali's harshness to the Timbuktu clergy was self-defence of the native religion. This is a clear case of a chronicle with a point of view (Module 4 lesson 3: local chronicles) and matches the Sunni/Askia debate; Diop's reading is plausible but is itself an interpretation. Also gives Askia Muhammad's pilgrimage (about 1,500 men, 300,000 gold pieces, 100,000 as alms, a hostel in Medina): another set of numbers to treat like Musa's, tagged as chronicle figures, not exact.

Diop claims that all of precolonial Africa was covered by monarchies and empires ('no spot, even in the virgin forest, escaped monarchic authority'), that Africans never knew a lay republic, and that every African is 'at heart an aristocrat'. Course Module 5 lesson 4 covers non-state societies (Igbo, others) and Module 1 gives Jenne-jeno's heterarchy; these directly contradict the first claim. The 'aristocrat at heart' remark is an essentialist stereotype. Trust the course's evidence-based position and show Diop's claim as a thesis with its two weak points. He himself allows a 'tribal Africa' of clans next to a monarchic Africa on the same page.

Diop argues the Lebou state on the Cape Verde peninsula (1795 onward) was a hereditary theocratic monarchy of the Diop family, not a republic, with a list of rulers to 1861 (French intervention). A useful correction of an old label, based on his own genealogical argument and 19th century records; the Diop-family list is a single-author claim I cannot check. Minor for the course; not added.

column4: ch-006 chunk 3 (Chapter 4, origins of the constitutional regime)
column5: Diop's own account of how consultative councils arose: court professions became hereditary offices; councils grew by social necessity; 'no text forced the king to take advice'. He calls this an inference ('We have tried to show...'). Present as Diop's hypothesis; the Mossi and Cayor evidence is 19th-20th century, so the historical depth is unproved.

column4: ch-006 chunk 4 (Chapter 4, courts of Ghana and Mali)
column5: Diop retells al-Bakri's account of the Ghana king (only king and heir in tailored clothing, gold-capped, pavilion audience, dogs with gold collars, drum signal, sister's son as heir) and Ibn Battuta's Mali audience (herald Dugha, silver-foiled windows, 300 soldiers, parasol with a golden bird). Matches course Module 4 lesson 1 (al-Bakri 1068 from informants, twin towns) and the Ibn Battuta lecturer lesson (court description). Adds al-Idrisi's claim of a glass-windowed castle built in 1116, which even Delafosse doubted: a good extra example of a distant geographer's detail. In the OCR the date '1706' for the Ghana king's insignia is an OCR or edition error; do not use.

column4: ch-006 chunk 4 (Chapter 4, Songhai court and insignia)
column5: Songhai oath-swearing on the Koran as the key act, Askia Muhammad receiving a green cap, turban and sabre from the Abbasid caliph in Egypt, tin-touri ember, the herald (wanado), dust on the head for audiences, Askia Daud (accession 24/03/1549) against the Mansa of Mali at Dibikarala (1559, as given by Diop: the course does not date this), Askia Daud marrying the Mali ruler's daughter. Dates are from the chronicles; I could not check them against the Arabic text. Not essential; keep one line in Module 4 lesson 3.

Diop presents an Almoravid conquest of Ghana in 1076, ten years of occupation ending with the death of Abu Bakr ibn Umar in 1087, and says 'goods looted, inhabitants slaughtered'. Course Module 3 lesson 2 'Did the Almoravids destroy Ghana?' tags the debate [CONTESTED]. Diop is reporting the traditional account, citing al-Bakri; the 'conquest' reading rests on later sources (Ibn Khaldun, Ibn Abi Zar). Keep the course's [CONTESTED] tag; add Diop as an example of the traditional reading.

column4: ch-007 chunk 1 (Chapter 5, Ghana's size and date)
column5: Diop claims Ghana's Black emperors ruled for 1250 years over a country 'as vast as all Europe', with 200,000 warriors (40,000 archers) in al-Bakri's day, ten thousand meals daily, and Berber and Arab merchants at Awdaghust governed by a Black farba (990). The 1250 years and 'size of Europe' have no firm source; the 200,000 is a figure from al-Bakri's informants (course l1: he never visited). Use as a numbers example in Module 4 lesson 2: tag as a reported figure, do not repeat the 1250 years. Confirms al-Bakri's Awdaghust information and the Ghana-Awdaghust relationship only at the level of one chronicler's report.

Diop quotes Hamidullah, summarising al-Umari (d. 1348) and the Atlantic voyage, and says Eastern annals noted that Kankan Musa gave only 20,000 gold pieces as alms in the two holy cities, against 100,000 by Askia Muhammad. This conflicts with the popular picture (Olivier: Musa gave gold so freely Cairo's price fell) and the course's cautious wording. A real disagreement of sources about numbers: show the three claims side by side and say not to resolve it by averaging; the safest statement stays: Arabic sources describe lavish giving, with figures that vary and cannot be treated as exact.

Ibn Khaldun on Mansa Musa's authority to Ouargla, an interpreter from Takrur in Cairo, a Moroccan embassy with gifts to the Mali ruler, Musa lending aid to an Arab emir on return from Mecca, two Arab jesters at Musa's court, al-Sahili building at Gao (as Diop writes 'Es Sakli'). A fair summary of the Arabic reports on Mali's diplomacy; checks against Olivier's popular account at only a few points (Gao mosque via al-Sahili is in both). Diop's inference that whites never ruled over blacks is a thesis.

column4: ch-007 chunk 2 (Chapter 5, no Arab conquest south of the Sahara)
column5: Diop says there was no Arab conquest of Black Africa, East Africa or the Sudan before the Moroccan war of 1591 (his dates: 16th century) and that Arabs entered peacefully. Course Module 3 lesson 2 covers the Arab conquest of North Africa and the baqt with Nubia, and Module 6 the Swahili coast origins debate (no conquest). Largely consistent for the Sahel and Swahili coast; but Diop is too absolute, ignoring Almoravid military pressure and conquest of Egypt/Nubian raids that led to the baqt. Show the point as his thesis [CONTESTED] with a narrow valid core.

Taxes, customs and gold: al-Bakri's customs on salt (one gold dinar per salt-laden mule entering, two per load exported, five mithqals per load of copper), the king keeping gold nuggets while the people keep dust (a 15 lb nugget inherited by the Mali ruler and sold by Mansa Djata, said to be Musa's grandson, per Ibn Khaldun), Bambuk mines, Timbuktu-Koi dispute with Tuareg Akil over three thousand mithqals. Good concrete figures for a Module 4 lesson on taxation and gold; the nugget-for-the-king rule is also in Olivier ch. 3 (miners keep dust) and is the one detail where both books use the same source tradition (al-Bakri/Ibn Khaldun). Treat as reported by chroniclers; the dinar and mithqal rates are not checked against the Arabic text.

Diop writes that 'Ali-Kolon, the future Sonni Ali' escaped Mali as a hostage and founded the true kingdom of Gao. Olivier's glossary treats Ali Koleni as one of two princes (with Sulayman Nar) taken by Musa in 1325 who escaped after Musa's death and began the Songhai dynasty, whereas Sonni Ali reigned from c.1464, about 140 years later. The two books disagree on who the hostage was; the dates cannot both hold if Sonni Ali is the 1464 ruler. Do not teach Diop's identification; say the sources conflate early Sunni dynasts and mark [TRADITIONAL DATE]. I did not check the Tarikh es-Sudan text (not ingested).

Diop derives Sudanic titles fari, farba, fama from Wolof per and the Egyptian 'Pharaoh' and argues the first West African states carried an Egyptian political memory 'by way of Nubia'. Pharaoh comes from Egyptian per-aa (great house) and the Mande/Songhai/Hausa/Wolof 'far' forms are short, similar words with no demonstrated sound correspondences. Same weakness as his Wolof-Egyptian comparisons in the other book; use as the Module 1 example of the linguistics blind spot (shared vocabulary needs regular correspondences) and tag [CONTESTED].

Diop argues that large states needed writing and records, citing letters Askia Daud wrote to his brother and his brother's mother, the Moroccan letter on the Taghaza salt mines seen by Sa'di, Askia Ishaq's reply with two iron boots. Strong, and consistent with the course's lesson on internal African written sources (Module 1 lesson 2, Timbuktu chronicles). Concrete anecdotes (iron boots, two letters) are chronicle details I can only check against the Tarikh es-Sudan, which is not ingested; use sparingly.

column4: ch-007 chunk 3 (Chapter 5, army and the Moroccan invasion)
column5: Songhai army: cavalry, infantry with bows, royal guard, Niger flotilla; gold-bracelet elite who would not flee; Songhai's defeat by Judar Pasha's firearms (Diop dates Judar's first battle during Askia Daud's time in his text, the course gives Tondibi and after). Diop's claims that Africans lacked firearms because merchants withheld them and that the 'first firearms exploded' are assertions without a source in the text; and Askia Ishaq II's reign is the one in which the Moroccans came. Show the fact (firearms gave Morocco the edge) and flag his two claims as unsupported. The Sonni Ali siege of Djenne (seven years in Sa'di, six months in Kati) is a perfect worked example of two chronicles disagreeing; Diop's 'truth lies in the middle' is not a method; the course's method is to tag [CONTESTED] and give both.

column4: ch-007 chunk 3 (Chapter 5, Cayor warfare and griots)
column5: Cayor knights charged individually and used crude firearms; Lat Dior adopted guerrilla tactics against Faidherbe; griots as battlefield exhorters. Nineteenth-century material beyond the course's date limit; mention at most as evidence that oral traditions about earlier Cayor are only reliable for the colonial period.

Two courts (royal justice and the qadi), ordeals by water and fire, qadis appointed and sometimes removed by the Askia (Kati versus Sa'di disagree on how much), notarised inventories drawn up by Sa'di himself (he was a notary and saw the prisoner Salti), and Ibn Battuta's praise of Mali's justice and the safe-keeping of dead merchants' goods. Confirms the course's Timbuktu chronicles and Ibn Battuta material; the Sa'di notary anecdote adds a firm example of the chronicler's role as a record-keeper. Note again that Diop quotes Ibn Battuta twice (Module 4 uses one).

Diop writes that the Atlantic slave trade 'swallowed up one hundred to three hundred million individuals, dead or shipped to America' and that Africa's population would have been about 400 million without it. Course Module 8 quotes the Voyages database (about 12.5 million embarked, with the source named), the figure now standard. Diop's range is not supported by any dataset I know of and is an order of magnitude above the Voyages records; trust the Voyages numbers and work the difference with the course's 'who counted it and how' rule. Rodney in the other book also discusses estimates; compare there.

column4: ch-008 chunk 1 (Chapter 6, Africans and the caravans)
column5: Diop says that camel caravans across the Sahara were an Arab initiative, that Africans never traded abroad and traded only at the domestic markets of Djenne, Timbuktu, Walata, Awdaghust and Gao, and that economic abundance made this unnecessary. Course Module 3 lesson 3 treats trans-Saharan trade as a network with Sahelian merchants (Wangara/Dyula, Soninke) and Berber caravaners; Diop himself earlier named the Wangara merchants (Tarikh al-Fattash) and Nunghamarta traders. Internal tension: he describes whole trading groups but then says Africans took no commercial initiative abroad. Show both and tag [CONTESTED]; the course's network model fits the evidence.

column4: ch-008 chunk 1 (Chapter 6, silent trade and money)
column5: Silent trade with gold-producers (Herodotus for the Carthaginians, Ibn Yaqut/al-Idrisi, with the Lem-Lem of the Faleme) and the range of currencies: salt blocks, cowries (500 to 3,000 per mithqal), gold dust measured by a mithqal he gives as about 4.6 g, copper rings, cloth squares (chigguiya), unmarked 'sola' dinars, and Ibn Hawqal's 40,000-dinar debt note between Sijilmasa and Awdaghust (10th century). Olivier ch. 12 attributes silent trade to Mali's gold-traders without a source; Diop places it with peripheral peoples and cites Herodotus and the Arabs: the better-sourced version. The 4.6 g mithqal and cowry range are Diop's; I cannot check them here (the usual figure for a mithqal is about 4.25 g, outside these books). Good additions for Module 3 lesson 3.

Diop gives 7,077 villages around Djenne (Sa'di), a Gao census of 7,626 house blocks under Askia al-Hajj, ten thousand daily meals at the Ghana court (Kati), a three-day student census of Gao. These are chronicle numbers; the course says to ask who counted them. Use them in the Module 4 numbers lesson as a second family of figures beside Musa's pilgrimage figures. Diop uses them to argue abundance and density 'scarcely imaginable today': a thesis, not a measurement.

Long summary of Marx on English enclosure, vagrancy laws and the birth of capitalism, used to argue African precolonial economies were at the stage of 'pigmy property' with caste monopolies and no expropriation of peasants. Out of scope; the claim that capitalism did not arise endogenously in Africa is the book's thesis and links to Rodney's argument in the other book. Not used in lessons; one sentence in the Module 8 'Rodney as one position' lesson could mention Diop's Marxist frame.

Diop describes slave settlements of the Askias (the Diam-Uali, Diam-Tene and Sorobanna groups farmed their own land and gave a fixed share; twenty-four slave groups taken over from Sonni Baro; an Askia slave making the pilgrimage unnoticed) as evidence that African slaves had conditions 'incomparably superior' to white slaves in Europe, and says the lot of Africa's slaves worsened after contact with Europe. The first part is a comparison with no measure; the second matches Module 8's account of the Atlantic demand reshaping slavery (Thornton and Manning would differ in degree). Use the Songhai settlement detail as one concrete form of slavery within Africa for the 'other slave trades' section; tag Diop's comparison [CONTESTED].

Detail from the Tarikh al-Fattash (via Diop): twenty-four slave 'tribes' inherited from Mali by the Askias, taxes in labour, grain, fish, spears and arrows; plantations run by slave managers (fanfa) with hundreds of slaves (the Abda estate: 200 slaves, 1,000 sacks of rice); manumission deeds; Askia Daud bartering some tribe children for horses; the king inheriting soldiers' goods. Gives concrete content for the Module 8 comparison of slavery inside Africa and the claim that structure was not simply benign: Diop himself concedes that slaves could be sold at any moment and that children were exchanged for horses. Cite as a detail from chronicle sources, reported by Diop; the figures (e.g. 4,000 sacks of grain) not checked.

Diop suggests commercial minorities like the Dyula parallel Phoenicians or Genoa as groups specialising in trade because of poverty or smallness; this supports the course's picture of Dyula/Wangara as a trading network. His 'African collectivism vs European individualism' explanation of economic differences is a generalisation to be tagged [CONTESTED], not taught.

column4: ch-009 chunk 1 (Chapter 7, Almoravids and Islam's spread)
column5: Diop retells the Almoravid beginnings (Yahya ibn Ibrahim, Abdallah ibn Yasin, a ribat, Ibn Khaldun's quotation 'a thousand men cannot easily be beaten') and says Islam in West Africa then spread mainly by peaceful traders, scholars and African rulers (Mali's convert king Barmandana, Djenne's Konboro, Askia Muhammad). Matches the course's Module 3 treatment of the Almoravids as a militant movement of Sanhaja and the later Sahelian pattern of conversion by rulers; Diop's 'only time white troops imposed Islam' repeats the old Almoravid-conquest reading the course tags [CONTESTED] (see the other finding).

column4: ch-009 chunk 1 (Chapter 7, Songhai Islam and the Dia legend)
column5: The Dia dynasty's origin from 'Dja men el Yemen' (a brother who defeated the river 'demon-fish' king) is a clear example of an Islamic-era legitimising origin story, parallel to the Solomonic story in Module 2 lesson 4 and the Sherifian origins Diop calls 'Sherifism'. Also Askia Muhammad's conflict with Sonni Baru (fifty-two days of negotiation, Salih Diawara), the qadi Mahmud refusing the Askia's envoys. Good source-critique case for the founding-myth checklist (Module 5 lesson 5) with a Sahel example; Diop says these legends 'altered the authentic history', his claim that a Nile migration is 'beyond doubt' is not shown.

Diop repeats that Meroe's Sudan was the 'Birmingham of antiquity' with eighty-four pyramids standing, and says modern Muslim Sudanese feel shame at the Meroitic past. The course (Module 2 lesson 2) already marks the Birmingham claim [CONTESTED] as overstating Meroe's iron industry, and gives over 200 pyramids in Sudan as a whole. Another case where Diop reproduces a popular claim the course corrects; use as a quick example of repeating a claim from a prestigious source. The 'shame' claim is a generalisation without evidence.

column4: ch-009 chunk 2 (Chapter 7, religion in Black Africa)
column5: Closing points: Islam in West Africa superimposed on existing political structure with indigenous titles, multiple sects (Tijani, Murid; Murid shrine in Touba instead of Mecca), and Diop's judgment that Arab chroniclers recorded African history 'with praiseworthy objectivity'. That last statement conflicts with the course's tags on al-Bakri, al-Umari and Ibn Battuta as distance sources with their own aims; teach the course's version (no chronicler is neutral). Twentieth-century Murid detail outside the course period.

Diop describes Timbuktu's 'university' of Sankore as a set of mosque-based schools run by qadis and scholars without an official building or pay, repaired in 1569 by Qadi al-Aqib and helped by Askia Daud, with 150 to 180 Quranic schools (Kati). He does not credit Mansa Musa with founding it. This agrees with the course's cautious treatment (no founding by Musa) and contradicts Olivier's 'founded by Mansa Musa'. Strong evidence for refining the course's Module 3 lesson 3 sentence on Timbuktu's scholars: the 'university' was an informal network of mosque teaching.

Diop cites Sa'di's chapter of seventeen Timbuktu scholars (logic, grammar, rhetoric, law), diplomas written by teachers (ijaza), Ahmad Baba said to have left over 700 works, Askia Daud buying a dictionary for 80 mithqals and employing copyists. Adds depth to Module 3 lesson 3 (Ahmad Baba, manuscripts). The 700-works figure is the usual number but it is a figure passed down by tradition; label it so. Diop's 'trivium and quadrivium' framing imports a European model; Sa'di himself names fiqh, grammar, logic and the like.

column4: ch-010 chunk 1 (Chapter 8, historical method of Kati and Sa'di)
column5: Diop shows Kati and Sa'di working like historians: citing authorities, dating events to the day and sometimes hour, questioning informants from Mali and Kanaga about a clan name, asking for a mutilated safe-conduct to be read, and Sa'di lamenting the decline of historical science in his own day. Matches the course's presentation of the Tarikh es-Sudan and Tarikh al-Fattash as internal sources (Module 4 lesson 3). Diop's claim that the dates were verified 'exact in almost all cases' needs a source; the course keeps dates approximate. Also Kati's attribution of his findings to a friendly genie is a good small case of the supernatural in chronicles.

Diop lists African scripts: Vai syllabary (Sierra Leone/Liberia), Bassa cursive, Nsibidi, Cameroon Bamum script (Njoya) and claims common signs with Egyptian. The Vai and Bamum scripts are known to be nineteenth-century inventions (Vai c.1830s, Bamum c.1896), which Diop half-admits ('may be of recent date'); his Egypt-link is unsupported. The course's Module 1 lists ajami and Ge'ez as African written sources; Nsibidi is a real local sign system. Add one line on indigenous scripts, with the invention dates marked as outside these books.

Diop dates the Sudanese-Moroccan war to 1593 and tells the Sankore round-up of 20/10/1593 and deportation of scholars to Marrakesh on 18/03/1594 (Ahmad Baba among them), the replacement of Judar by Pasha Mahmud ibn Zarqun, Askia Nuh's resistance in Dendi, and the 'armas' of mixed descent. Course Module 3/4 places the invasion in 1591 (Tondibi) and Ahmad Baba's deportation after it. Both are right about different events: Tondibi in 1591, the crackdown on the scholars 1593-94; Diop's heading '1593' for the war is loose. Add the 1593-94 repression as a dated event from Sa'di, tagged as reported by Diop, and fix any lesson that merges the dates. I have not checked the chronicle.

Diop says tons of documents are lost, with manuscripts perhaps dormant in family libraries and archives (300 items awaiting translation at an institute since 1900). The course gives 300,000 to 700,000 manuscripts as a [CONTESTED] range. Diop's text predates the modern Timbuktu manuscript projects (1960) and gives no count; so it supports 'lost and dormant' but not the numbers. Keep the course's range-and-tag treatment.

Koranic schooling from age 4 or 5, recitation by about 11, pre-Islamic age-set initiation (circumcision camps, 'locals'), Sa'di's remark that Timbuktu scholars could hardly ride camels when fleeing Sonni Ali. Rich ethnographic detail from 20th-century Senegal projected backwards; useful only as a caution against the same projection that Module 1 warns about (oral tradition and present-day practice can be read back).

column4: ch-011 chunk 1 (Chapter 9, as-Sahili and Sudanese architecture)
column5: Diop quotes Ibn Khaldun's report from Musa's Arab companion that as-Sahili (Abu Ishaq al-Tuwayjin) built a square, domed, plastered reception hall at the capital, and argues that (a) it was a hall, not a mosque, so the story that as-Sahili built the Gao mosque goes beyond the text, and (b) the 'Sudanese style' (oblong, buttressed, no cupola, no arabesques) is not what Ibn Khaldun describes, hence not imported by him. This directly contradicts Olivier ch. 14-16 (as-Sahili introduced mud brick and the Malian style, built mosques in Gao and Timbuktu and a palace in Timbuktu) and fits the course's modest 'patronised mosque-building in Timbuktu and Gao'. Show both: Ibn Khaldun's hall at the capital is the firm datum; the style attribution is argued by Diop and rests on his reading; also Kati calls the claim that Musa built a mosque in every Friday village groundless. Trust the Ibn Khaldun passage over Olivier; mark Diop's style argument [PROBABLE].

Askia Muhammad captured 500 masons at Jaga in 1495 (kept 400, sent 100 to the Kanfari's capital Tendirma); Bonnel de Mezieres's 1911-13 digs at Kumbi (houses of several storeys, 30 cm walls), Ibn Battuta's wide straight avenues at Niani, the Tamberma fortified houses, Dogon cliff houses, al-Idrisi's 1116 castle again. Good links between written sources and archaeology for Module 4 lesson 1 (Kumbi Saleh and Tegdaoust). Diop is honest that Bonnel de Mezieres may not have found the capital itself; Mauny's later digs (cited in his bibliography) are not in this book.

Diop repeats Hamidullah on al-Umari's story (200 ships, then 2,000 under the ruler who handed power to Musa) and says Columbus's crew reported Blacks in the Americas, pirogues from Guinea, and 'guanin' metal; he thinks contact was constant. The course (Module 4 lesson 2) tags Mande-American contact [CONTESTED] and rejected by most archaeologists. Diop's position is the minority one; no archaeological find of West African origin in pre-Columbian America has been shown in these books. He also gives the first expedition as 200 ships, whereas Olivier gives 400 ships then 2,000: the sources differ on the first fleet. Show the numbers difference as another example of how numbers vary between retellings.

Diop says Great Zimbabwe's builders were Bantu (Caton-Thompson, Venda), excavations yielded only Bantu-type skeletons, and the Phoenician/Solomon theory is 'once and for all invalidated'. Agrees with the course's Module 7 position that the colonial myth is false, but the claim is stated with weak evidence (skeleton typology). Use the course's archaeological case; note Diop's confident statement as an agreeing voice. His description 'cover an area as large as France' is an exaggeration.

Diop describes an 'astrolabe' and astronomical observatory at Meroe from Lepsius's drawings and a Birmingham-of-antiquity comparison citing Leclant; the observatory and astrolabe claims are unsupported by modern excavations (the scene Lepsius drew is a ritual/other). Same [CONTESTED] Birmingham claim as in the other chapter; correct as the course already does.

Diop says maize and tapioca (cassava) reached Africa before Columbus via return voyages from the Americas, citing Van Sertima (1977) as leaving 'no doubt'. Maize and cassava are generally treated as arriving in Africa after 1500 through Portuguese and later Atlantic trade, with no archaeological evidence of earlier arrival in the sources here; Van Sertima's thesis is widely rejected (outside these books, not verified here). Course Module 8 can use the Columbian-exchange crops as an Atlantic effect; mark Diop's claim [CONTESTED] and unsupported.

Diop derives the Yoruba (Lucas), Laobe (from the Sao), Peul, Tukulor, Serer, Wolof clans from the Nile through matching ethnic and clan names (Kan, Wan, Ka, Ba, Karé, Kau-Kau) and Egyptian words (ka, ba), and reads the Tundi-Daro standing stones as a Serer migration marker. These are sound resemblances among short, common syllables with no regular correspondences and with 20th-century clan names matched to ancient Egyptian words; the claims that the Yoruba lived in Egypt or that Egyptian gods survived in Yoruba are unsupported. Module 5 lesson 4 (myth as evidence; Oduduwa) and Module 1 (Bantu expansion, Nok-Yoruba [CONTESTED]) already warn against such origin claims; add this as a worked example for the founding-myth checklist (who tells it, what evidence, what is the alternative) and tag [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-012 chunk 1 (Chapter 10, Pygmies and tall Blacks)
column5: Diop says tall Black people had not yet peopled West Africa in the fifth century BCE and that earlier remains were 'Pygmy', and that the whole continent was partly peopled by Pygmies, then 'Black mankind' radiated from the Nile after the Sahara dried c. 7000 BCE. Current work (Module 1 lesson 3: Bantu expansion from Cameroon/Nigeria, Nok, Jenne-jeno) shows West African farming and iron-using societies in the first millennium BCE and earlier Holocene occupation; Diop's 'tall Blacks' vs 'Pygmies' scheme is early-20th century racial typology. Trust the course.

Diop (citing Kati) says the Sonni and Askia rulers came from the Upper Senegal region (Askia Muhammad's father Arlum Silla from Silla), not from Berbers or Yemenites, and that Sa'di wrongly made Adior/Wolof Berbers. The course treats Songhai origins through Sa'di and Kati and the Dia legend; the question is disputed and Diop's reading selects one chronicle's inquiry. Tag [CONTESTED]; useful as an example where two chronicles (Sa'di and Kati) give different origins.

Diop reads the Tundi-Daro stones as fertility-cult phalli of Sky and Earth (Eliade), says the Serer migration marks the Egyptian route, says Sonni Ali was mummified and Serer burials resembled Egypt's, and derives the Agni from Anu/Oni, the Bamum cult of the king from Egypt, and Wolof clan names from the Nuer and Sara lists. Chance name-matching of the same type as the other chapters; the stones are not dated or linked to Serer in these books, and the Maes quote he used is an earlier colonial denial of African authorship. Tag [CONTESTED] and do not teach as fact.

The English edition omits the French 'Linguistic Appendix' on Wolof, Serer and Peul class languages, so the book's linguistic argument is not testable here. The Postface lists UNESCO colloquia Diop proposed (peopling of Egypt, Meroitic decipherment, migrations/toponyms/ethnonyms) and says the first four were held. The bibliography is mostly 19th and early-20th century: Arabic sources in French translation (de Slane, Houdas, Delafosse; al-Bakri, al-Idrisi, Ibn Battuta, Ibn Khaldun, Sa'di, Kati), colonial ethnography (Tauxier, Desplagnes, Maes, Pedrals), Marx and Fustel, and Van Sertima (1976). The Arabic-source quotations are the book's strongest evidence; the comparative and linguistic argument is its weakest. This is a fair, balanced sentence for the Module 1 historiography box.
